Question: A 47-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of skin lesions on his lower extremities, accompanied by fatigue and progressive numbness and weakness in his right hand. He denies abdominal pain, cough, or shortness of breath. His medical history is notable for a past incarceration of 10 years and homelessness since his release last year. He has a history of intravenous drug use but has been abstinent for the past 5 years. He is up-to-date on vaccinations. On examination, he is alert and oriented, with a temperature of 38.1ºC (100.6ºF), pulse 90/min, respirations 15/min, and blood pressure 148/88 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals palpable purpura on the lower extremities and decreased muscle strength, reflexes, and sensation in the right upper extremity. Peripheral pulses are intact bilaterally, and there is no pedal edema. Chest auscultation is unremarkable. Laboratory studies show:

| Hemoglobin | 13.5 g/dL |
| --- | --- |
| Leukocyte count | 11,500/mm³ |
| Platelet count | 265,000/mm³ |
| Serum |  |  |

| Cl⁻ | 102 mEq/L |
| K⁺ | 3.9 mEq/L |
| HCO₃⁻ | 25 mEq/L |
| Total bilirubin | 0.9 mg/dL |
| Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) | 88 U/L |
| Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) | 96 U/L |
| Creatinine | 1.6 mg/dL |
| HIV | Negative |
| Hepatitis B surface antigen | Negative |
| Hepatitis C antibody | Positive |
| HCV RNA | Positive |
| C3 complement | 59 mg/dL (N = 72–120) |
| C4 complement | 0.5 mg/dL (N = 14–40) |

Transient elastography indicates mild hepatic fibrosis. What is the most appropriate initial step in managing this patient?
Answer Choices: (A) Systemic corticosteroids alone (B) Interferon therapy (C) Plasma exchange therapy (D) Intravenous immune globulin therapy (E) Rituximab monotherapy (F) Cyclophosphamide pulse therapy (G) Combination therapy with ribavirin and sofosbuvir (H) Direct-acting antiviral therapy (I) Plasmapheresis with albumin replacement (J) Immunosuppressive therapy

Options:
A. Systemic corticosteroids alone
B. Interferon therapy
C. Plasma exchange therapy
D. Intravenous immune globulin therapy
E. Rituximab monotherapy

Physical findings include mild peripheral and facial edema, normal respiratory exam, and no neurological deficits. His gait is steady.

Question: A 65-year-old man arrives at the emergency department with sudden onset of shortness of breath that began while he was working on his car at home. He had been exposed to various chemicals and inhalants while repairing the engine. His symptoms did not improve with rest, and paramedics transported him to the hospital, where he is now receiving 100% oxygen via nasal cannula. The patient has a 52-pack-year smoking history, drinks 2–3 alcoholic beverages nightly, and has a history of asthma but has not seen a physician since high school. His vital signs are as follows: temperature 98.2°F (36.8°C), blood pressure 157/108 mmHg, pulse 120/min, respirations 29/min, and oxygen saturation 77%. Physical examination reveals tachycardia with a systolic murmur best heard at the right upper sternal border, diminished breath sounds over the right upper lobe, and bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Answer Choices: (A) Acute right heart failure (B) Rupture of an emphysematous bleb (C) Tension pneumothorax (D) Chemical pneumonitis from inhaled toxins (E) Methemoglobinemia from chemical exposure (F) Acute exacerbation of underlying COPD (G) Right-sided pulmonary embolism (H) Bronchial obstruction from mucus plugging (I) Pulmonary edema secondary to decreased cardiac output (J) Fe3+ hemoglobin in circulating red blood cells

Options:
A. Acute right heart failure
B. Rupture of an emphysematous bleb
C. Tension pneumothorax
D. Chemical pneumonitis from inhaled toxins
E. Methemoglobinemia from chemical exposure
F. Acute exacerbation of underlying COPD
G. Right-sided pulmonary embolism
H. Bronchial obstruction from mucus plugging
I. Pulmonary edema secondary to decreased cardiac output
J. Fe3+ hemoglobin in circulating red blood cells
